name: Finding Collaborators
title: Finding Collaborators
answer: Finding collaborators for grant proposals is the work of identifying people, groups, and institutions whose expertise, resources, or access complements a proposed project. It covers co-investigators, senior personnel, external partners, community organizations, industry collaborators, and international teams. The aim is to assemble a team that funders will see as credible and capable, not merely to add names to a proposal. This topic sits inside grant proposals and funding, and it connects to the wider research practice of team science.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Finding collaborators for grant proposals is the work of identifying people, groups, and institutions whose expertise, resources, or access complements a proposed project. It covers co-investigators, senior personnel, external partners, community organizations, industry collaborators, and international teams. The aim is to assemble a team that funders will see as credible and capable, not merely to add names to a proposal. This topic sits inside grant proposals and funding, and it connects to the wider research practice of team science.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on public and institutional research profiles, publication databases, co-authorship records, and funder award histories. Common sources include ORCID, Google Scholar, ResearchGate, university research office directories, and conference proceedings. AI tools for expertise matching and graph analysis can help surface potential partners from large publication networks. Institutional research development offices often maintain internal databases of prior grants and available facilities.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical process starts with a clear statement of the expertise and resources the project needs, then searches literature, funded project databases, and conference programs for people who match. Researchers often trace co-authorship networks, ask trusted colleagues for introductions, and meet potential partners at workshops or society meetings. Once a shortlist exists, the work turns to conversations about scope, roles, budget, data sharing, and authorship. AI-assisted matching can rank candidates by topic similarity, but human judgment and direct conversation remain central to forming a working team.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in finding collaborators include privacy, consent, accuracy of publication records, and the proper use of personal data from profiles and directories. Institutions and funders usually require disclosure of conflicts of interest, current and pending support, and any related financial interests. Provenance matters when a match is based on automated analysis, and teams often need to trace why a person or group was suggested. Collaboration agreements, data use agreements, and authorship plans are typically handled by research offices and legal counsel, not by the matching tool itself.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward persistent identifiers, richer graph data, and AI systems that recommend teams rather than individual authors. Funders increasingly encourage or require interdisciplinary and multi-institution collaborations, which pushes institutions to build better expertise maps. At the same time, concerns about bias, privacy, and over-reliance on automated matching are likely to shape how these tools are governed. The practical result may be faster discovery of potential partners, with human review still deciding who actually joins a proposal.
